accroche: She knows all the physics of color. She has never seen a color. What is she missing?
contenu_vulgarise:
Mary is a brilliant neuroscientist. She has spent her entire life locked in a black-and-white room, where she has seen only shades of gray: the walls, her clothes, even the screen through which she observes the outside world. But her specialty is precisely color vision, and she knows everything about it: the wavelengths that strike the retina, the chemical reactions in the cones of the eye, the neural circuits that fire when a human brain looks at a tomato and says the word “red.”

The Australian philosopher Frank Jackson, who imagined this scenario in 1982 in an article titled *Epiphenomenal Qualia*, then asks the question that gives the experiment its full weight: the day Mary leaves her room, or a red tomato is slipped before her eyes, does she learn something new?

## The Trap of the Obvious Answer

The answer that comes naturally is yes. Finally seeing red teaches her what it is like to see red: an experience that no physics formula, however complete, had conveyed to her in black and white. But if she learns something that day, then her knowledge before was not complete. Yet she possessed, by hypothesis, absolutely all the physical information about color vision.

Jackson draws a radical conclusion: there is therefore information that is not physical in nature, and physicalism (the idea that every fact, mental facts included, reduces in principle to physical facts) is false. The lived experience of a color, what philosophers call qualia, would thus escape any third-person description, however detailed.

## What This Shifts

The argument immediately provoked rejoinders. Some physicalists answer that, on leaving, Mary acquires not new knowledge about the world but a new ability: that of recognizing red, imagining red, remembering it, a know-how rather than a knowing-that, which in no way threatens the idea that every fact remains physical. Others maintain that she does acquire knowledge, but under a different presentation of a fact she already knew in another form.

Jackson himself would change his position years later, finally rallying to the physicalism he had wanted to refute. This reversal does not close the debate: it mainly shows that the experiment's most solid intuition, that something is missing for Mary, withstands scrutiny far better than any argument meant to explain it, including that of its own author.

repere.texte: Jackson published the Mary experiment in 1982, in a ten-page article titled Epiphenomenal Qualia, on pages 127 to 136 of the Philosophical Quarterly. He later revisited his own conclusion, finally declaring himself a physicalist.
repere.source: Frank Jackson, The Philosophical Quarterly, vol. 32, no. 127, 1982

carte.punch: She knows everything about the physics of color. She has never seen a color.
carte.idee: In 1982 Frank Jackson imagines a scientist locked in black and white, who knows all the physics of vision. The day she finally sees red, does she learn something? If so, physics does not say everything.

quiz.question: According to Jackson's thought experiment, what does the day Mary finally sees a color reveal?
choix: That she had poorly memorized some of the physical knowledge she already had
That colors do not really exist in the outside physical world
That her confinement in black and white had altered her perception of colors
That the physics of vision, however complete, does not suffice to describe the experience itself
quiz.explication: Mary possessed, by hypothesis, all the physical information about color vision before leaving. If finally seeing red nonetheless teaches her something, it is because this complete physical information was not enough to convey the lived experience of color: not that she had forgotten a detail, that colors would be unreal, or that her perception would be distorted.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What conclusion does Jackson draw from his thought experiment, in the 1982 article?
choix: That there is non-physical information, which makes physicalism false
That color vision is impossible to describe scientifically, even in part
That Mary will never be able to recognize red, even after leaving her room
That neuroscience must give up studying color perception
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Jackson concludes that there is information that is not physical in nature, which makes physicalism false, the idea that every fact reduces in principle to physical facts.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do some physicalists answer to Jackson's argument, according to the text?
choix: That Mary never really lived locked in black and white
That the color red does not exist in the outside physical world
That Jackson misdescribed the wavelengths of red light
That Mary acquires a new ability, not new knowledge about the world
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Some physicalists answer that Mary acquires only an ability, recognizing or imagining red, a know-how that does not threaten the idea that every fact remains physical.
